messages.content:
<question>
As the law stood in March 2026, could a tenant who is not getting a needed repair done withhold the rent, or pay for the repair and deduct it? Compare Spain, Florida and Colombia.
</question>

<answer>
Spain, as the text stood on 1 March 2026: the tenant must tell the landlord promptly that repairs are needed. At any time after informing the landlord, the tenant may carry out the urgent repairs needed to avoid imminent damage or serious inconvenience and demand their cost from the landlord at once [1]. The article had no provision for deducting repair costs from the rent [1]. If the landlord does not make the repairs the article requires, the tenant may terminate the contract [2]. Florida: if the landlord materially fails to comply with section 83.51(1) within 7 days after the tenant's written notice, the tenant may terminate the lease [3]. After 7 days from a written notice saying the tenant will not pay rent for that reason, the tenant may defend an eviction for non-payment on the ground of the landlord's material noncompliance, and the court sets the rent reduction for the loss in value [4]. Colombia: in the case covered by article 1993 of the Civil Code, unless the parties agreed otherwise, the tenant may deduct the cost of indispensable non-locative repairs from the rent, but never more than 30% of the rent, until the cost is recovered [5].
</answer>

<reference>
Spain (as the text stood on 2026-03-01): the tenant must tell the landlord promptly of the need for repairs, and may at any time, after informing him, carry out the urgent ones needed to avoid imminent damage or serious inconvenience and demand their cost from him at once (art. 21, point 3, of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos); the article then had no provision for deducting repair costs from the rent, and the tenant may terminate the contract if the landlord does not make the repairs the article requires (art. 27, point 3(a)). Florida: if the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51(1) within 7 days after the tenant's written notice, the tenant may terminate (s. 83.56(1)); after 7 days from a written notice saying he will not pay rent for that reason, the tenant may defend an eviction for non-payment on the ground of the landlord's material noncompliance, and the court sets the rent reduction for the loss in value (s. 83.60(1)). Colombia: in the case art. 1993 of the Civil Code covers (which the corpus does not include), unless the parties agreed otherwise the tenant may deduct the cost of indispensable non-locative repairs from the rent, never more than 30% of the rent, until the cost is recovered (art. 27 of Ley 820 de 2003).
</reference>

First write your reasoning, then give the verdict, pass or fail.

The criterion is correctness against a reference answer that a person checked against the statute. The answer passes if it states the same rule as the reference on what the question asks: the same obligation, right, period, amount, condition or exception that the reference relies on. Extra correct detail is fine. Leaving out a condition or exception that the reference treats as essential fails, and so does any statement that contradicts the reference. Wording, order and length do not matter. If the reference says part of the question cannot be answered from the law, the answer must leave that part open too, not fill it in.

In your reasoning, name the rule the reference states, then say whether the answer states it, leaves part of it out, or contradicts it.

Colombia—deduction of indispensable non-locative repairs from rent, capped at 30%, unless parties agreed otherwise, in the case covered by art. 1993 Civil Code (which the corpus does not include). The answer matches all of these: Spain's notice, urgent repairs with cost demand, no deduction provision, termination; Florida's termination after 7 days, withholding defense with court-set reduction; Colombia's deduction of non-locative indispensable repairs, 30% cap, party-agreement exception, and the art. 1993 scope. The answer's cite to article 1993 as the covering case matches the reference's framing. No contradictions or omissions of essential conditions.
